anchors.fact: In 2002 Nick Blacknell, who had worked with Ford at Seagram's, sent him to New York to hand-sell Plymouth gin. When Blacknell took the brand over, it was down to five thousand cases a year (*A Proper Drink* p. 109; card F3).
anchors.meaning: Sent in where nobody was waiting for him.
anchors.speaksTo: the one true thing (am I one of you?)

anchors.fact: Simonson: Ford "laughed after every other sentence and was hard to dislike" (p. 110; F4).
anchors.meaning: What they show: ease, a grin.

anchors.fact: Ford said he "never once sold a bottle". Instead he asked bartenders if he could teach them about his gin and about bartending (p. 110; F6). It's his own account of his method, not a sales figure.
anchors.meaning: The ask said out loud, not a trick.

anchors.fact: When Jim Beam took over Plymouth's distribution, they "wanted nothing to do with whatever a brand ambassador might be". Blacknell's deal: "Give him three months". "Ford stayed." (p. 111; F7). They rejected the role, not him by name.
anchors.meaning: Handled like a stranger, and someone who knew him vouched.

anchors.fact: Of the trips' cost, Blacknell said Ford "probably didn't tell me how much it cost" and "I didn't really mind; he was doing a good job" (p. 111; F9). It's Blacknell's guess, said afterwards.
anchors.meaning: Someone in charge suspected, and didn't mind.

anchors.fact: Ford convinced Plymouth to invite a handful of American bartenders to its distillery in England. A kind of travel followed in which "Humble drink-slingers" who'd never been offered "so much as car fare" were flown to Cognac, Kentucky, Jerez and beyond (p. 111; F8). Oxford: the model "was copied and employed across the liquor and bar industries" (pdf 828; F2). The page doesn't order the trips against Beam's takeover.
anchors.meaning: The rule bends for the whole table.

anchors.fact: Oxford gives two aims together: the brands' influence, and the bartenders' "education and professional standing" (pdf 828; F2).

Plymouth's revival: Murphy and Rolls's investors bought it in 1998 and restored it. Oxford credits Plymouth's "support for the modern cocktail revival", see FORD, SIMON (pdf 1541; P1). Ford's link to this gin is on the page. Today's ABV is unsourced (P2).
anchors.meaning: It's his gin, but not his rescue alone.
anchors.speaksTo: the drink: the story in the glass

anchors.fact: The French 75 is "essentially, a Champagne or 'Imperial' Tom Collins". The traditional recipe is strained "into a highball glass filled with cracked ice". Arnaud's flute (served up, with cognac) is "counter to the original recipe" (Oxford pdf 850–851; P4). The Codex: "Some bartenders prepare a French 75 in a tall glass with ice"; the Codex itself uses a flute and Plymouth (p. 142; P5).
anchors.meaning: The ice that makes someone wince was in the original. The legend gets granted, then corrected.
anchors.speaksTo: the drink; truth with a wink

anchors.fact: Until the 1840s champagne was "preferred sweet", and "If too sweet, it was best served almost frozen". The first recorded Champagne Cocktail (Panama, 1855) had ice (Oxford pdf 427; I1–I2).
anchors.meaning: Older than the rule people quote. Never "the rule is younger": no page dates a rule.

cocktail.closingLine: Ice first, whoever's watching. Then pour the rest of the bottle for the table.
cocktail.glassware: large wine glass (about 500 ml), filled with ice
method: Fill a large wine glass right to the top with ice. Yes, for Champagne.
Shake the gin, lemon and syrup hard with ice for about five seconds, just enough to chill it.
Strain it over the ice in the wine glass.
Pour in the Champagne slowly, then lift it once with a spoon to mix.
Squeeze the lemon peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.
Pour the rest of the bottle for whoever's with you.
cocktail.name: Just This Once

recipe.note: or any dry gin of 40–43% (for a 44% gin, use 45 ml)
or any brut (dry) sparkling wine; the rest of the bottle is for the table
squeezed over the top, then dropped in

cocktail.tagline: You don't get away with things. You get let off. That's better.

reading.epigraph: The man sent to sell the gin in this glass said he never sold a bottle.
whoYouAre: It's ten past ten, and the kitchen closed at ten. You go up to the counter, make the cook laugh, and five minutes later there are chips for six. The doorman, the receptionist, the teacher at the gate: you've had a yes out of every one of them, and you asked to their face.

People say you get away with everything. You don't. You get let off, which is different: someone decided to, because it's you. Every "go on, then" is a small proof you're still wanted. What you dread was never the telling-off. It's the one who doesn't look up, says "rules are rules", and handles you like a stranger.

There's a code in it, though you'd laugh at the word: you only try it on someone who can afford to say yes. And here's what you never get credit for. When a rule bends for you, it bends for everyone you came with.
yours: When Nick Blacknell was brought in to save Plymouth gin, it was down to five thousand cases in a year. He sent an old colleague, Simon Ford, to New York to hand-sell it. Ford said he never once sold a bottle. He asked bartenders, "Can I teach you about my gin?" He was, by one account, hard to dislike.

An American whiskey company took over selling Plymouth and wanted nothing to do with whatever his job was, so Blacknell bargained for three months. Ford stayed. He talked Plymouth into flying a handful of American bartenders to its distillery in England. On the bills, Blacknell said: "Knowing Simon, he probably didn't tell me how much it cost… I didn't really mind; he was doing a good job."

That's the sentence I'd frame. Somebody guessed, and didn't mind. And those trips spread: bartenders who'd never been offered so much as a bus fare were flown to Cognac, Kentucky and Jerez, and the idea was copied across the trade. I like to think he never forgot who'd let him off. That's you. A yes you win is never only for you.

The cocktail I've made for you is a French 75, a renowned Champagne classic, made with Plymouth, the gin he said he never sold. It breaks a rule people love to quote: the Champagne goes over ice, a whole wine glass of it. Somebody will wince. They needn't. The original recipe went over cracked ice, in a tall tumbler. I've made it a little sharper and sweeter than the flute version, so it stays balanced as the ice melts into it. The rest of the bottle goes round the table, as a nod to those trips: when Ford got a yes, other people came along.

Keep asking. It works, and whoever says yes enjoys it more than they let on. But now and then, ask for something you're owed, plainly, with no grin and no "go on". Watch the yes come anyway. The people who let you off were never doing it for the charm. They like you.
